chapters.summary: Council Member Chi Ossé discusses the disbandment of the NYPD Strategic Response Group and calls for passage of the Curb Act to codify bans on kettling, tear gas, and pepper spray.
chapters.title: Council Member Ossé calls for passage of Curb Act

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: When I first ran for office, one of my priorities was to end the city's reliance on the anti-democratic, violent strategic response group, most notably separating responsibilities relating to counterterrorism and protest activity.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: One of the first bills I introduced in this body aimed at addressing that problem, the Curb Act.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: This week, alongside Mayor Mamdani, we finally disbanded the Strategic Response Group.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: The newly announced changes to the NYPD's patrol guide are based on provisions of the Curb Act, a bill for which I am honored to have received support from the mayor on.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: While we have achieved disbandment, the work still continues.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: It's time we and the city council do our part and pass the Curb Act.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: My legislation will codify the mayor's policies into law, ensuring that the disbandment of the SRG lives on past the Mamdani administration.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Throughout history, the council has precedence in passing laws that codify mayoral programs.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: programs and actions, such as Intro 56 in 2022, which codified Mayor de Blasio's life-saving Narcan Behind Bars program, and Intro 1137 in 2018, which codified Mayor Michael Bloomberg's

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Office of Data Analytics.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: We also codified a bill this year, Intro...

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: 580A, which established the permanent office of child care, which was created under Mayor Adams.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: We should see no reason to treat the Curb Act differently.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Second, the Curb Act will only strengthen the mayor's protest policies.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: It would strengthen the NYPD's prohibition on using harmful tactics such as kettling, use of tear gas, and pepper spray by tightening or explicitly clarifying their ban at protests and demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: It would add more reporting requirements to ensure better transparency for the NYPD's protest response going forward.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: The disbandment of the SRG is not solely the end of a chapter of violent violations of First Amendment rights by police, but also the beginning of something new.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I hope other colleagues who are not signed on, please sign on, and I hope it comes to a hearing very soon.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Thomas Henry, followed by Hanif.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shanel Thomas-Henry speaks on the Flatbush building collapse and introduces Intro 1198 requiring DOB to notify local officials within 24 hours of serious stop-work orders.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry introduces Intro 1198 on DOB stop-work notifications

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I rise today to introduce legislation that gets to the heart of what good government should do.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Protect our neighbors, respond to their concerns, and hold those responsible for their safety accountable.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Just last week, we witnessed the devastating building collapse in Flatbush, and my colleague, Councilmember...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Member Farrah Lewis's district.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Families have been left grieving, neighbors have been displaced, and an entire community is searching for answers.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And while investigations continue, one thing is clear.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: While we build, New Yorkers should never have to question whether the buildings they live in, work in, or walk past are safe.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Development is inevitable, but it cannot be at the expense of putting our neighbors at risk.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That is why I am proud to introduce legislation to strengthen transparency, communication, and accountability at the Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Intro 1198 requires DOB to notify the local council member and borough president within 24 hours of issuing a stop work order for a Class 1 or Class 2 violation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It also requires weekly reports detailing outstanding violations, penalties, stop work orders that have been issued or lifted, and the reasons those orders were rescinded.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because when a building raises serious safety concerns, the people elected to represent that community should not be the last to know.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We should have the information necessary to ask questions, demand answers, and advocate for our neighbors before another tragedy strikes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And let me be clear, this is about making sure the safeguards we already have are working for the people they were designed to protect.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This is about building accountability into the foundation of how our

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: city grows.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to join me in supporting this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson, followed by Lewis.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carl Wilson proposes requiring Citi Bike operators to verify users' ages with government or school IDs after a fatal crash involving a 15-year-old.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson introduces Intro 1200 on bike share age verification

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Today, I'm introducing a bill, Intro 1200, that would have operators of bike share programs like City Bike verify users'age with government or school-issued IDs.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The bill would also allow DOT to explore other methods of age verification while considering privacy concerns.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Currently, city bike users must be at least 16 years old to ride, but this policy is weakly enforced and easy to bypass.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: This can end in tragedy, as was the case earlier this autumn when a 15-year-old city bike rider who attended the museum school in my district died after colliding with a truck.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Advocates agree that these age limits need to be enforced more strongly with safety and privacy foremost in mind.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I invite my colleagues to join me in supporting this endeavor.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Farah Louis describes the Flatbush building collapse, thanks Speaker Menin and colleagues, and supports Council Member Thomas-Henry's Intro 1198.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis recounts Flatbush collapse and supports DOB notification bill

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Members Lewis, followed by Zhuang.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Last week, our district experienced an unimaginable tragedy when a building collapsed in Flatbush, claiming the lives of eight individuals and left close to 19 others critically injured.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Behind every number is a person, a family, and a community whose lives have been forever changed.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Families are being forced to navigate grief and uncertainty and the difficult road to rebuilding their lives.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I am proud.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: to have worked closely with community partners on the ground to connect directly with families to help them understand their needs and to support them with resources.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Amid the pain, there were two glimmers of hope.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: A woman, six months pregnant, was buried in debris, and both she and her baby survived and are doing well.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And the cat.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Of 11-year-old Zaria Isaac, was rescued days later thanks to the efforts of Flappish Katz and Ali from OME.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Speaker Julie Menon for standing with our community and for advocating for stronger legislation and protections, and I'm grateful to my colleagues who reached out to extend condolences and support.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Today, I am proud to stand with Councilmember Thomas Henry in support of her bill, Intro 1198, to require DOB to notify local council members and borough presidents within 24 hours of issuing certain serious stop work orders and provide

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: reasons for when those orders are lifted.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Our communities deserve to know when buildings are unsafe, and we must do everything to ensure that no New Yorker ever has to endure this crisis again.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Council Member Susan Zhuang discusses the Sunset Park fire and rising battery-related fires, introducing Intro 1202 to lower the violation threshold for shutting down retailers.
chapters.title: Council Member Zhuang introduces Intro 1202 on e-bike battery safety enforcement

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Zhuang, followed by Marano.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Over the past months, my heart has been with the families of six people we lost in devastating Sunset Park fire.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: These were six people who should still be with us today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: As a representative of this community, this tragedy is deeply painful.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We cannot allow any family to experience this kind of loss.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The investigation is still going on, but the iron batteries were found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This is a growing citywide concern.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Battery-related fires jumped from 241 last year to 406 this year.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Tomorrow, the City Council will hold an emergency hearing on resident fire safety and the battery storage.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But we need more than just answer.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We need action.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Today, I'm introducing Intro 1202 to make it easier for cities to shut down retailers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Repeatedly violating e-bike and the battery safety law.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Currently, it takes three violations within three years.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: My bill will lower that to just two violations within two years.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: After the first violation, businesses have been warned.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They must be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Our families deserve to feel safe in their homes and our streets.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We cannot wait for another tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to support Intro 1202.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Public safety must come first.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano proposes requiring developers to disclose homeless shelter plans before receiving building permits, citing the Arthur Kill Road shelter proposal.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano introduces Intro 1194 on homeless shelter disclosure

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilor Marano, followed by Narcis.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you're building a hotel, tell us you're building a hotel.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you're building a homeless shelter, tell us you're building a homeless shelter.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't think that's too much to ask, and that's why today I am introducing Intro 1194, which would require developers of certain construction projects to disclose

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: whether they intend to operate a homeless shelter before they're granted a building permit.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They'd have to tell us how many people the shelter would house, what population it would serve, and if known, who would operate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That information would be posted publicly and sent to the local council member, borough president, and community board.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If the plans materially changed during construction, they'd have to update that information.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This legislation grew out of my fight against the proposed homeless shelter on Arthur Kill Road in my district, and I've had to spend an extraordinary amount of time trying to get basic answers to some remarkably ordinary questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if a member of the city council has this much trouble getting information, imagine what it's like for the average resident or the average homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: My colleagues may disagree with me about where homeless shelters belong, and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But surely we can agree that the people who live in a neighborhood are entitled to know what's being built there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And unfortunately now, that's just not the case.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You shouldn't need a law degree, a FOIL request, and a friend at the Department of Buildings to find out what's going up across the street.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This is a good government bill, and I hope my colleagues on both sides of the aisle will join me in sponsoring it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Intro 1194.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Mercedes Narcisse introduces a resolution honoring Pierre Damas Bell, a Haitian honor student who died by suicide after being fitted with an ICE ankle monitor, and calls for policy change.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse honors Pierre Damas Bell with Reso 742

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilwoman Arcees, followed by Jay Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing Reso 742, a resolution in honor of Pierre Damas Bell.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Pierre Damas, every time I call his name, I just...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He came to this country from Haiti to get an education.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He was an honor student.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He quickly joined JROTC, which is a military-sponsored program that provides training for students.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He was playing soccer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He was living a life of a young person.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And he held a GPA of 3.8, which he was very proud of.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He had no criminal record.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In July, ICE put an ankle monitor on him.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He asked twice to have it taken off, please.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: He stays on him.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: His father said they put an ankle monitor on him and everything changed.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: On September 1st, Pierre called his father to say he was struggling.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: A few hours later, he died by suicide.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: His family is still suffering, and we cannot forget that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This month.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: President Trump said himself that he went too far with deportation policy.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So now he's already gone.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So this policy, thank you, Madam Speaker, put it on.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We need to look forward to see how we address this, especially with young people with no criminal record, have a 3.8 GPA, and joining the military training program and doing everything that he could have done.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We could have saved him, but unfortunately, we can save others.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Justin Sanchez discusses environmental injustice in the South Bronx and introduces a bill to ban transport refrigeration units from running at warehouses.
chapters.title: Council Member Sanchez introduces bill banning stationary TRU use at warehouses

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Jay Sanchez, followed by Epstein, then Feliz.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Throughout my career in advocacy, government, and now as a council member, I've come to realize that the problems I grew up seeing in the Bronx were no accident.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They were the result of deliberate decisions about where to invest, where to neglect, and who would be left to bear the burden.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: For too long, the people who shaped our city chose to push the problems they didn't want to deal with into the corners of the city they would never have to visit, let alone call home.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And what makes it worse is that many of the people living in these communities already have the deck stacked against them.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yet time and time again, they're asked to shoulder even more.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: These are the corners of our city where real people live, where resources never reach us, where parents sleep four hours a night because they have 20 hours of work ahead of them, and where children grow up carrying the burdens they never asked for.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: These injustices are not just in our history books.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The decisions that shaped our neighborhoods decades ago are still shaping our lives today, and they're still in effect now.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We talk a lot about undoing them, but they have not yet been undone.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So in an agreement that would take a step forward,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: just becomes undone at the one-yard line and gets swept under the rug that would finally provide justice and finally help generations of South Bronx families breathe cleaner air.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's frankly insulting.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I refuse to let another broken promise go unsung, and I refuse to let this go ignored.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: That is why I'm introducing legislation to ban the stationary use

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: use of transport refrigeration units, or TRUs, at warehouses across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: These diesel-powered units are meant to refrigerate goods during transport.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Instead, some warehouses leave them running 24-7 a day, pumping pollution into our neighborhoods, rather than investing in proper refrigeration that meets the needs of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They're once again tucking away the problem and pushing onto communities already carrying more than their fair share.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Enough is enough.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The days of passing the buck are over.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: This bill puts an end to using TRUs and all of the pollution and hardship they have brought.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Council Member Harvey Epstein introduces the CHAT Bill requiring AI disclosure and a human option within 15 minutes, and a bill requiring human staffing at gyms and spas.
chapters.title: Council Member Epstein introduces bills on AI customer service and gym staffing

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Council Member Epstein, followed by Felice, then Caban.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm proud to be introducing two bills that will improve safety and transparency for customers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The first one is called the CHAT Bill, Customer Help Accountability and Transparency, requiring large businesses to disclose when they're using AI for customer service.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Providing users with an option to speak to a human representative, and provide customers with the option to connect to human customer service agents to make a good faith effort to do so within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We've all been waiting on hold for hours to try to get through someone at a store, and they keep saying representative.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We need to change that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: A second bill I'm introducing is inquiring staffing at gyms, spas, make sure there's at least a human employee, especially where the public goes in.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's no human staffing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It potentially can be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We talked about this in different...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: opportunities, especially when business hours are open.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We need to make sure that it's safe for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I encourage my colleagues to look at these two bills.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I encourage you to sign on.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Oswald Feliz proposes prohibiting the placement of live animals into boiling water, saying lobsters remain on the menu but must be killed first.
chapters.title: Council Member Feliz introduces bill banning boiling live lobsters

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilor Felice, followed by Gavan.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: As a city council, we have a responsibility to address issues affecting New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Issues related to public safety, education, housing, opportunity, and so much more.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We must prioritize and work to resolve these issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Prioritizing these issues, however, does not mean that we should overlook issues that may not affect us directly and personally, including animal rights issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So today I'm proud we've

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: all introduced a host of many different bills, just for purposes of diversifying the agenda, I am proud to introduce a bill to strengthen animal rights issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Some might find it funny, but I hope that we could at least start the conversation on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Let's ask ourselves, how wild would it be to boil a live animal?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It would be beyond wild, right?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And unfortunately, it's the norm for many animals, including lobsters, lobsters that are boiled alive before they're consumed.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It's wild, but it's also not necessary.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Some argue that lobsters don't feel pain, but if they don't feel pain, then why is it that they start making sounds and they make every effort to jump out and escape when they're being boiled alive?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Boiling an animal alive, that is the textbook definition of animal cruelty and something that I hope we could start the conversation about.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I also want to be crystal clear, this bill will not

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Under any circumstances, remove lobsters from the menu.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Everyone is still obviously able to consume all the lobsters that they want.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This bill will simply require that the lobsters be killed before being boiled.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Prohibit the placement of a live animal into boiling water.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Everyone who knows me knows I'm a very fair council member, so I look forward to starting the conversation and engaging with stakeholders, including small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're obviously going to be listening to them very carefully.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm sure they're going to have very concerns, and I look forward to speaking with them.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And again, as a city council, we have a responsibility to address issues that people care about.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I've had the privilege of working on many issues, public safety, e-bikes, fire safety, so much more, and I look forward to...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Working on this issue just because it doesn't affect us directly doesn't mean that we should overlook it.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Council Member Tiffany Cabán condemns Amazon's $5 delivery fee pop-up as corporate extortion and defends the Delivery Protection Act's licensing fee and safety standards.
chapters.title: Council Member Cabán responds to Amazon's delivery fee threat over Delivery Protection Act

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Kavan, followed by Linda Lee.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Today, Amazon gave us a prime example of corporate bullying and corporate greed.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: This morning, if you opened up an Amazon app, you saw that they served this pop-up that said that they were going to start charging New Yorkers $5 for every delivery if we passed the Delivery Protection Act.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And first, I want to thank the speaker for her leadership and clearly repudiating this nonsense and what essentially amounts to corporate extortion.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But here's the thing that I want to be clear about.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The math simply isn't mathing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Let's make this clear.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The Delivery Protection Act, it requires a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It would require a company like Amazon to pay a $500 licensing fee every other year

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: to cover the millions and millions and millions of packages that get delivered every single day in this city, and would also require them to abide by the most basic of safety standards for its workers and for people across our city.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That in no way, no matter how you do the math, amounts to charging $5 per order per New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: This is simply about a $3 trillion company saying that we don't care about safety on our streets, we only care about our profits, and we will lie to you and extort you to those ends.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We've seen this playbook before.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We've seen it from Uber and DoorDash.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: pass those protections for the deliveristas that were much needed.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's dishonest, it's sleazy, and they're trying to scare consumers.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But we're New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We know junk when we see it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And we're not going to be bullied.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We're not going to be threatened.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We're going to pass this bill, and we're going to make our streets and our workplaces safer for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And thank you for the co-sponsors on this bill that have stayed strong on it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We are going to get it done.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Council Member Linda Lee introduces Intro 1191 requiring written billing requirements and Intro 1192 requiring the city to reimburse interest when registration delays force nonprofits to borrow.
chapters.title: Council Member Lee introduces bills on nonprofit contract registration and interest reimbursement

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Lee, followed by Brewer, then Ressler, then Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Our city relies on neighborhood nonprofits to deliver essential services in New York.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Picture one of those nonprofits.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It turns in its paperwork, its staff are out delivering meals, providing legal services or mental health services, but the city is still working to register the contract and payday is Friday.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So the nonprofit takes out a loan to pay its staff.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Even after the city pays, the nonprofit still owes the bank interest.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing two bills.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: First one is Intro 1191 about what happens when you send the city an invoice.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Imagine you've done the work and followed the instructions and then an agency asks for a record it never told you to keep.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Now you're piecing together paperwork while you wait to get paid.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Under this bill, agencies would have to put their billing requirements in writing when they sign a contract.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: To change those rules or ask for extra records later, they'd need the city's chief procurement officer to sign off first.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: The second bill, Intro 1192,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: would cover that borrowing cost.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: If the city's own registration delay forces a nonprofit to borrow to keep services running, the city would pay it back for reasonable interest and lender fees.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: People who do the city's work need to understand what is expected and not have the rules change in the middle of the budget process.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I encourage all my colleagues to sign on to both these bills.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer introduces Intro 1185 to expand the city's reproductive health safe harbor to contraception, fertility treatments, IVF, miscarriage management, and telehealth.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer introduces Safe Harbor Act expansion

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilor Brewer, followed by Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Safe Harbor Act is Intro 1185, and it would expand the city's reproductive health safe harbor law for the first time since the act was enacted in 2022.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know in that year, following the horrible decision of overturning Roe v.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Wade, the city council enacted Local Law 74.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Prohibiting the use of city resources to assist other states in investigating or prosecuting people for obtaining or providing lawful abortion care.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Since then, our state has strengthened its shield laws, but this bill also brings New York City's law in line with those protections.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It expands the city's safe harbor to include contraception, fertility treatments, IVF, miscarriage management, pregnancy care, and telehealth services.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know that people are still coming to New York City for reproductive health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: According to the DOH, 25% of contacts to the city's abortion access hub came from outside of our state.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 35% Florida, Texas, and Georgia, for example.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Under this proposal,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: proposed law, city employees and other resources cannot be used to detain people for receiving or providing reproductive health care

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that is legal here or to share identifying information with out-of-state authorities seeking to enforce their bad restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: New York City must protect patients and providers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to thank

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Public Advocate Williams, Councilmember Hudson, my co-chair, Councilmember Joseph, Councilmember Farias, for co-priming this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thanks to Noam Yovsky, Legislative Counsel, and most particularly Cynthia Hornig, Director of Budget and Legislation in my office.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just also want to say I do not like those goddamn...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Electric carriages proposed for the park.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler proposes requiring large new buildings to have waste treatment facilities and a bill to designate appointees to recommend wage increases for lowest-wage workers.
chapters.title: Council Member Restler introduces bills on sewage overflow and collective bargaining equity

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Councilmember Ressler, followed by Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer is always a tough act to follow.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There are about 21 billion gallons of polluted water and raw sewage, or just poop, that goes into our waterways each and every year in our waterfront city in New York.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And that's because about 60% of our sewer infrastructure is combined infrastructure for both wastewater and for sewers, as a sewer treatment.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, you know, we put billions of dollars every so often into these long-term control plans to try to improve the water quality in places like Newtown Creek or the Gowanus Canal or tributaries all around the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we're nowhere near to having the cleanliness of water that we deserve.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so we need to think about new and different ways to reduce combined sewage overflow in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And one way we can do that is to require in large construction, not, you know, 10 or 20 or 50 unit buildings, but in large new buildings, that they have their own waste treatment facilities so that they're not sending their poops

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: into our sewer system that simply can't handle it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We all know that when there's a light rain for 30 or 40 minutes, you're supposed to not flush your toilet because who wants poop going into the East River?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That is not...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: not the infrastructure of a modern city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we need to think about new and creative ways to strengthen our regulatory frameworks, and this is one.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm also, that's 1195, I think, but you can look up the number.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're also introducing another bill today that we're calling kind of equity committee around collective bargaining, where we're asking the speaker and the mayor's office and the MLC to designate appointees

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: to look at the lowest wage workers in New York City and recommend wage increases for at least three titles a year that go above and beyond pattern bargaining.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Pattern bargaining fails the lowest wage workers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's why the Speaker pushed and Chair Carmen de la Rosa, Councilmember de la Rosa, pushed the RESPECT Act for paras.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is a new and different approach that would be incorporated into collective bargaining to strengthen wages for our lowest wage workers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Amanda Farías sends condolences to Council Member Mealy and calls on Speaker Menin to close the meeting.
chapters.title: Council Member Farías sends condolences and calls on Speaker

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin thanks Council Member Mealy and adjourns the stated meeting of November 19, 2026.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin adjourns stated meeting

summary: The New York City Council held a stated meeting on November 19, 2026, beginning with an invocation by Reverend Phillip Jackson and a roll call of members.
The Council voted on land use call-ups, general orders, multiple resolutions, and introductions, including bills on dental care, doula services, fertility treatment, and HPD registration.

Members also delivered remarks on local and international issues, honored individuals such as Bill Ritter and Pierre Damas Bell, and introduced new legislation on public safety, housing, and animal welfare.
